opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I try to be pretty sober about it, because it's easy to overclaim in either direction.

The clearest external signal we have is the ICLR workshop experiment. We submitted three fully AI-generated papers to the "I Can't Believe It's Not Better" workshop. The organizers knew about it, the reviewers didn't know which papers were AI-generated, and one of the three got scores that put it above the average acceptance threshold. We had agreed beforehand to withdraw any accepted paper, because the community hasn't yet settled the norms for this, and we didn't want to put AI-generated work into the record without that conversation happening first.

I'd add some caveats right away. It was a workshop, not the main conference, and workshop bars are lower. The paper reported a negative result: a compositional regularization idea that didn't work as hoped. That fits the workshop's theme, but it's also an easier kind of contribution than a strong positive finding. And when we went through the papers ourselves, we found real problems: citation mistakes, some imprecise claims, and figures or framing a careful human researcher would have tightened. So I wouldn't say these papers are at main-conference level yet. They aren't.

What I find scientifically interesting is less any single paper and more the trajectory and the process. Version one relied heavily on human-written templates. Version two drops most of that and uses an agentic tree search over experiments, so it can explore, debug, and branch without a human scaffold. Getting past peer review at all, even at a workshop, is a meaningful milestone for an end-to-end automated pipeline.

Peer review is also a noisy, imperfect measure of scientific value. A paper getting in doesn't make it important, and a rejection doesn't make it worthless. So alongside external review, we read the outputs closely ourselves and ask: is the hypothesis sensible, are the experiments actually testing it, are the conclusions justified by the evidence? That internal scrutiny is often more informative than the accept/reject bit.

My overall view is that the value right now is mostly as a proof of concept and a tool for exploring ideas cheaply and in parallel, especially in the long tail of experiments humans wouldn't prioritize. The open question is whether these systems can move from competent, incremental work to genuinely surprising, field-shifting ideas. I don't think we've seen that yet. That's where the hard and exciting research is.

r002.rationale: The response calls the system a proof of concept and a tool for exploring ideas, but does not say that it generates preliminary research for researchers to build upon.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the scientific value, right now, is modest, and I'd rather be upfront about that than oversell it. What we showed with AI Scientist v2 is a milestone in the process, not a milestone in the science. One of the papers passed through peer review at an ICLR workshop, and that's a genuine data point. It means the system can, end to end, formulate a hypothesis, run experiments, write it up, and produce something that reviewers judged as meeting the bar for a workshop. But a workshop acceptance is a fairly low bar, and the paper itself was, by any reasonable standard, an incremental contribution. Nobody's going to build on it the way people build on a landmark result.

So if you ask whether these papers advance machine learning as a field, I'd say not meaningfully yet. What they do is tell us something about the agents. The interesting part for me is where they fail. The system is actually decent at the mechanical parts: writing code, running sweeps, generating plots, producing plausible-sounding prose. Where it struggles is in taste. It doesn't have a good sense of what's worth asking, it over-claims from weak evidence, and sometimes it misreports its own results. We saw cases where the experiments didn't support the narrative in the paper, and the agent kind of papered over it. That's exactly what you don't want in a scientific process, and it's partly why we put so much emphasis on transparency, releasing the raw outputs and the reviews rather than just the headline.

I'd also push back on the framing a bit. The goal isn't to flood the literature with marginal papers. That would be actively harmful. The goal is to understand whether the loop can be closed at all, and then make each stage trustworthy, with humans still in the loop for the judgment calls. The right way to read v2 is as a prototype that tells us the plumbing works and that the bottleneck has shifted from "can it do it" to "can it do it well and honestly."

r002.rationale: The response calls the paper incremental and says nobody is likely to build on it. It presents v2 as a prototype for studying the research loop, not as a tool that generates preliminary research for researchers to build upon.

astra-6.text:
I would separate two things: can the system carry out a coherent research project, and does that project produce a significant scientific discovery? Those are quite different bars.

For me, the value is currently more in the first category. Can it formulate a hypothesis, design an experiment, implement it, interpret the results, and write something that other researchers can scrutinize? Getting that whole loop to work is meaningful. But a polished paper, or even an acceptance, doesn’t by itself establish that the underlying contribution is important.

You still have to ask: were the baselines appropriate? Do the experiments actually support the claim? Does the result survive replication? And is it telling us something we didn’t already know? We should apply the same standards that we apply to human research.

So I would treat these papers as early evidence of an automated research capability, rather than equate them with major discoveries. The stronger test is whether the findings hold up and become useful to other scientists.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to distinguish between producing a paper and producing a scientific contribution. A system can generate a plausible hypothesis, run experiments, and write up the results, but the scientific value depends on whether those experiments actually support the claim—and whether the claim teaches us something new.

So I would assess these papers individually. Are the baselines appropriate? Are the results robust across random seeds? Do the ablations isolate what’s responsible for the improvement? Could somebody independently reproduce the finding? A polished narrative doesn’t resolve any of those questions.

There’s also a separate question about what this demonstrates about automating research. You could have a paper with a relatively modest contribution that still represents meaningful progress in the system’s ability to carry out an experiment autonomously. That’s interesting, but we should keep those two judgments separate: how capable is the research system, and how valuable is the science it produces?
